rv.q: One joy in James Macdonald’s superb new production — led by stunning performances from Ben Whishaw and Lucian Msamati — is that it honours, so eloquently, the irony in that.
This is the best production I’ve ever seen.

James Macdonald’s production has tender moments, it’s often funny and gives plenty of scope to Whishaw - occasionally channelling his inner Paddington Bear - to be endearing without ever being cloying.
Macdonald’s revival forces you to listen and learn.
Sometimes, it feels like MacDonald’s production could sit a bit longer with this play’s discomfiting moments, especially in the first act.
James Macdonald has clearly scoured the text for its morsels of amusement and crumbs of comfort.

James Macdonald’s production, unfolding in the obligatory barren landscape with a blasted tree, is smooth and confident with welcome shafts of humour, but there can be no escaping the fact that Godot is long and gruelling in its repetitions and reiterations.
It’s not, perhaps, a revelatory staging, and its measured pacing demands patience and close attention.

Whishaw’s tremendous Vladimir is part man-child, part strident philosopher, part Pollyanna, his sparrow-like brightness barely concealing a desperate need to cling on to the certainty that Godot will arrive tomorrow, his long pianist hands forever madly gesticulating in hope.
Again, it’s a brilliant play, that you can’t do a lot to.
Anyone interested in the theatre will want to see Macdonald’s intricate, thoughtful staging.
The comedy works in itself, and so do the dramatic moments, but the two seem slightly disconnected.
Director James Macdonald unlocks its tensions with perfect poise, letting its seriousness and sadness emerge but also filling it with a surprising amount of love.
I have never seen this play so lucidly done.

Suffice to state that the play (which has so often been synonymous with overwrought performances, long pregnant pauses and unexplained angst) is delivered here with a level of wit, timing and sincerity which is rarely achieved in productions of Beckett’s complex and infuriating enigma.
This Godot is a bitter tragicomic farce, deeply philosophical but also genuinely funny.

Embracing, holding fast to each other like infants in a playground, what emerges from the chemistry between Wishaw and Msamati (both as fine dramatic actors as they are comic) is quite how much this production’s Didi and Gogo love one another.
Surreal and entertaining in equal measure, there may be some people who think this play is overrated.
While the stars bring marquee magnetism, the production design lends mystery.
A bit boring, of course, but there are laughs to be had in James Macdonald’s production.
Together, the four capture the play’s daft humour as they question, contradict and forget one another.
This is how you revive a classic and realise it to its full potential.

Rae Smith’s design is of an ashen earth populated by a petrified tree that turns out to be miraculously alive, and also by random passersby Pozzo (Jonathan Slinger), a heartless landowner and his gormless then unstoppably articulate slave Lucky (Tom Edden).
Macdonald’s production is poignant but never portentous.
Waiting for Godot proves to be as searingly relevant as ever.
A rare treat to find this work on a major London stage and for those with an appetite for Absurdist Theatre, the show is unmissable.

Whishaw and Msamati bring a humanity and comic believability to the characters in this James Macdonald (True West, Vaudeville Theatre) production that succeeded in warming our heart in a way that we weren’t quite expecting.

cn.t: Critics hail Macdonald's revival as a superb, utterly compelling production anchored by stunning performances from Whishaw and Msamati, who strike an ideal balance between Beckett's tragicomic absurdity and existential weight.
